chunks: GPU optimizations and trade-offs. The question: What optimizations does a GPU have so it vastly outperforms CPUs in graphics tasks? What are the tradeoffs?
GPU designers assume the work is millions of independent, similar pieces, and every optimization uses that.
Each instruction is fetched once and run on 32 small arithmetic units (lanes) at once, many threads take turns to hide memory delays, and the memory is very wide and fast.
Dedicated hardware handles common jobs. Each of these gives up flexibility for efficiency, so a GPU is poor at single tasks, branchy code and small jobs.
Think of a bottling plant. It is superbly efficient at filling millions of identical bottles: one control system runs a hundred filling heads, and the conveyor never stops.
But ask it to make one custom jar, or to handle bottles that each need different treatment, and it wastes most of its machinery. The speed comes from giving up flexibility.
The dashed line is the arithmetic floor E a = 4 pJ. With overhead 10x the arithmetic cost, widening the group from 1 to 32 lanes cuts energy per operation by 8. 4x.
Beyond about 16 lanes the gains flatten near the arithmetic floor, which is why going wider than 32 to 64 buys little but costs divergence.
Amortization: spreading a fixed overhead, such as fetching and decoding an instruction, across many operations.
Fixed-function unit: dedicated hardware for one job, such as texture filtering, that beats general code.
Divergence: lanes in the same group of 32 wanting to take different branches, which leaves some lanes idle ("How a GPU works").
Memory bandwidth: bytes per second between memory and the chip.
Use the page's illustrative energy numbers. Fetching and scheduling one instruction costs 40 pJ (picojoules, tiny units of energy), and the arithmetic itself costs 4 pJ.
A scalar machine, which does one operation per instruction, pays both for every operation: 44 pJ. A GPU sharing one instruction across 32 lanes pays 40 over 32 plus 4 equals 5.
25 pJ per operation. That is about 8. 4 times less energy. The trade-off: if branches leave lanes only 60% useful, the cost per useful operation is 5. 25 over 0. 6 equals 8.
75 pJ. That is still about 5 times better. That is the whole idea: each trick trades generality for efficiency.

"GPUs exploit massive independent parallelism: SIMT amortizes fetch and decode over 32 lanes, thousands of threads hide latency instead of caches, very wide memory like GDDR or HBM feeds them, and fixed-function raster, texture and blend units do common work very efficiently.
Compression and on-chip tiles cut bandwidth.
The costs are weak single-thread speed, divergence and memory-pattern sensitivity, huge register files and power, limited memory, and harder programming."
